pack: Pack 9 — expansion (AI, sustainability, Business Environment depth)

questions.stem: Your governance charter delegates change decisions to you up to 50,000 per decision, with an aggregate cap of 60,000 above which the change control board decides. Four variations of 12,000 each have been approved under your authority this year. A fifth variation of 12,000 has just been proposed, and the sponsor mentions she can sign it off today to save time. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: Thresholds apply to the sum of decisions, not just to each decision taken alone.

options.text: Route the variation to the change control board, since the aggregate of approved variations would reach 60,000 and the charter assigns that decision upward.
options.rationale: Each variation is individually within delegated authority, but the fifth takes the cumulative total to the aggregate cap, which is exactly the condition the charter reserves for the board. The per-decision limit is the trap the scenario is built around.

options.text: Approve the variation under delegated authority, since 12,000 is well within the 50,000 per-decision limit.
options.rationale: This is the one-decision-at-a-time error. It reads the per-decision limit and ignores the aggregate cap, which exists precisely to stop a series of small approvals quietly becoming a large unauthorised commitment.

options.text: Accept the sponsor's offer to sign the variation today, since her authority exceeds the project manager's.
options.rationale: This is the seniority-as-route error. A senior signature is not the same as the correct body, and the charter assigns aggregate breaches to the board as a collective decision with impact analysis, not to any individual.

options.text: Split the variation into two smaller requests so each remains comfortably within delegated limits.
options.rationale: This is threshold gaming, and it converts a governance question into an integrity one. Splitting a single change to evade an approval level is the specific behaviour aggregate caps are designed to catch.

questions.explanation: Delegated authority almost always has two dimensions: a limit per decision and a limit on the accumulation of decisions. Checking only the first is how governance thresholds get defeated by accident. The charter has already decided who should weigh a programme of change that has grown to 60,000, and the project manager's job is to recognise that the trigger has been reached and route the decision there, whatever the individual size of the next request.

questions.stem: Your developers have started using a generative AI coding assistant and report a clear productivity gain. You discover that prompts being sent to the external service include fragments of production code containing customer personal data. Your organisation has no policy on AI tooling, and the vendor's marketing describes the service as enterprise-ready. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: A useful tool handling regulated data is a compliance question before it is a productivity one.

options.text: Pause the flow of customer data to the service immediately, and engage security, legal and the data protection officer to establish approved usage before the team resumes.
options.rationale: Two things are true at once: the tool has value, and personal data is currently leaving the organisation's control with no assessment behind it. Stopping the data flow contains the exposure now; convening the right functions is what turns an ad-hoc adoption into a governed one.

options.text: Allow continued use with a reminder to the team not to paste sensitive data into prompts.
options.rationale: This is the policy-by-reminder error. The behaviour has already happened with the team unaware, and an instruction without an approved configuration, training or oversight repeats it the next time someone is in a hurry.

options.text: Prohibit the tool entirely and remove access until the organisation publishes an AI policy.
options.rationale: This is the ban-instead-of-govern error. It protects data at the cost of a demonstrated productivity gain, drives usage underground where it cannot be seen at all, and hands a policy vacuum back to the people who created it.

options.text: Obtain the vendor's enterprise-readiness statement and file it as evidence that the tool is compliant.
options.rationale: This is the marketing-as-evidence error. Enterprise-ready is a commercial claim, not an assessment of your data flows against your obligations, and filing it answers a question nobody with regulatory standing asked.

questions.explanation: AI tooling adopted bottom-up creates compliance exposure before anyone has decided anything, because the data flow starts the day the tool does. The project manager's move is to separate the two halves of the situation: contain the unassessed data flow now, and route the tool itself through the people who can approve a configuration, a data boundary and permitted uses. Neither blanket permission nor blanket prohibition does both.

questions.stem: Your project operates under a regulator that audits annually. Last year's audit found that controls were operating but evidence was assembled retrospectively each spring, at significant cost and with two gaps that could not be closed. Which two changes most reduce this year's exposure?
questions.mindset: Compliance you reconstruct afterwards is the most expensive and least reliable kind.

options.text: Design each control together with the record it produces, so evidence exists as a by-product of the control operating.
options.rationale: The audit finding was not that controls failed but that proof was manufactured after the fact. Building the artefact into the control removes the reconstruction step entirely, which is where the cost and the two unclosable gaps came from.

options.text: Assign each regulatory obligation a named owner with a review point in the project calendar, rather than treating compliance as a shared background duty.
options.rationale: Retrospective assembly happens when nobody owns an obligation until audit season. Named ownership with scheduled review turns compliance from an annual event into a continuous activity with a person attached.

options.text: Begin assembling the audit evidence two months earlier so the gaps are found with more time to close them.
options.rationale: This is the earlier-same-process error. Starting the reconstruction sooner still reconstructs, and the two gaps that could not be closed failed because the evidence never existed, not because the calendar was tight.

options.text: Hire an external compliance consultant to own the audit response this year.
options.rationale: This is the outsource-the-problem error. An external party can advise, but the obligations, the controls and the evidence live inside the project's daily work, and renting an owner for March does nothing about the other eleven months.

options.text: Add a compliance sign-off gate at the end of each phase, requiring the audit file to be complete before proceeding.
options.rationale: This is the end-loaded gate error. A phase-end check still batches evidence into events rather than producing it continuously, and it converts compliance into a schedule risk sitting at every phase boundary.

questions.explanation: The finding describes an evidence problem, not a control problem: the work happened and could not be proven cheaply or completely. The durable fixes are structural: make every control emit its own proof as it runs, and give every obligation a person and a date so nothing waits for spring. Earlier assembly, external owners and phase gates all accept the retrospective model and try to run it harder.

questions.stem: Last night, under your organisation's emergency change route, you authorised an urgent fix to a live settlement system with the on-call approver, and the fix succeeded. The emergency procedure requires the change to be documented and presented to the change board within five working days. The team wants to move straight on to the next priority, since the process was followed correctly. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: An emergency route is fast process, not less process — the record is what makes it auditable.

options.text: Complete the emergency change record with the decision and its authority, and present it to the change board for ratification within the required window.
options.rationale: The emergency route deferred the board's review; it did not cancel it. The ratification step is what converts a fast decision into a governed one, and the five-day clock is already running.

options.text: Take no further action, since the emergency procedure was followed and the fix is working.
options.rationale: This is the success-erases-process error. The procedure was only half followed: the authorisation half. The documentation and ratification half is also the procedure, and skipping it leaves the emergency route indistinguishable from a bypass in the next audit.

options.text: Raise a standard change request for the fix and wait for the board's normal cycle to approve it.
options.rationale: This is the wrong-instrument error. The change has already been made under the emergency route; a standard request asks the board to approve a past event through a channel designed for future ones. The procedure specifies ratification instead.

options.text: Note the fix in the next status report so stakeholders are aware it happened.
options.rationale: This is the announcement-instead-of-record error. A status report is communication, not control; it does not capture the authority under which the change was made or give the board its ratification decision.

questions.explanation: Emergency change provisions trade sequence for speed: authorisation comes first and the board's review follows after. Organisations that use the first half and skip the second accumulate changes that were urgent, successful and ungoverned. Completing the record and obtaining ratification is what keeps the emergency route trustworthy enough to be used again.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the average elapsed days at each stage of your project's procurement approval chain, measured over the last quarter. Your sponsor wants approval cycle time reduced and has suggested chasing suppliers to respond faster. Select the TWO stages that together show where the constraint sits and which stage is being starved by it.
questions.mindset: A queue marks the constraint; emptiness behind it marks the starvation it causes.

graphic.title: Procurement approval chain, average days per stage, left to right
graphic.caption: Select two stages. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Specification ready — 1 day
regions.rationale: One day is fast and internal. Nothing accumulates here and nothing waits on it, so it is neither the constraint nor its victim.

regions.label: Budget check — 1 day
regions.rationale: A one-day automated check is flowing freely. It sits upstream of the constraint but clears its work as fast as it arrives.

regions.label: Legal review — 9 days
regions.rationale: Nine days against one day everywhere else is where work accumulates. The constraint is internal to the organisation, which is why chasing suppliers — the sponsor's suggestion — cannot touch it.

regions.label: Finance sign-off — under 1 day, mostly idle
regions.rationale: A stage that is fast and mostly idle, sitting directly behind the queue, is the starvation signature. Finance has capacity it cannot use because legal releases work to it in batches.

regions.label: Purchase order issued — 31 this quarter
regions.rationale: A completion count accumulates by design. Thirty-one issued orders tells you the chain delivers, not where it waits.

questions.explanation: Constraint identification reads the pattern, not a single number: a large queue in front of a stage and idle capacity behind it. Here both point at legal review, an internal stage. The sponsor's instinct to pressure suppliers addresses the one part of the chain with no waiting in it. The effective responses follow from the reading — adding review capability, pre-agreeing standard contract terms, or reducing what must go through legal — rather than pushing harder at the ends.

questions.stem: A quantified threat on your register has a probability of 30 per cent and an impact of 120,000. A proposed response would cost 50,000 and reduce the probability to 10 per cent; the impact would be unchanged. Work out the figures below, using a minus sign if a figure is negative.
questions.mindset: A response is worth its cost only when the exposure it removes exceeds what it costs.

blanks.label: Current expected monetary value of the threat
blanks.rationale: 0.30 × 120,000 = 36,000. This is the exposure the register currently carries against this threat.

blanks.label: Expected monetary value if the response is taken
blanks.rationale: 0.10 × 120,000 = 12,000. The response reduces the exposure by 24,000, not to zero — the threat can still occur.

blanks.label: Net economic effect of taking the response (exposure removed minus its cost)
blanks.rationale: 24,000 removed minus 50,000 spent = −26,000. The response destroys value in expected terms, so on these numbers it should not be taken — acceptance or a cheaper response is the sound strategy.

questions.explanation: Expected monetary value turns a risk register from a list into an economics exercise. The trap in this class of decision is comparing the response cost with the full impact (50,000 to prevent 120,000 sounds attractive) rather than with the exposure actually removed, which is the change in EMV. Here the response removes 24,000 of expected loss at a cost of 50,000, and the correct decision is to decline it — a conclusion only visible once the arithmetic is done.

questions.stem: At the retrospective, the team proposes reducing review batch sizes to shorten cycle time. In previous quarters, two improvement ideas were adopted with enthusiasm and later found to have made no measurable difference; a third was quietly abandoned after making things worse. Which two actions should accompany this proposal?
questions.mindset: An improvement is a hypothesis until a measure says otherwise.

options.text: Agree before starting which measure will judge the change, its current baseline value, and what result would count as success.
options.rationale: The two failed improvements were adopted without a test that could have falsified them. Fixing the measure, the baseline and the success threshold in advance is what turns an opinion into an experiment with an answer.

options.text: Timebox the trial and review the evidence at a set date, keeping, adjusting or abandoning the change on that basis.
options.rationale: The third improvement failed silently because nothing ever reviewed it. A review date forces the keep-or-kill decision into the open and prevents an ineffective practice becoming permanent by default.

options.text: Implement the change across all teams simultaneously so results are comparable.
options.rationale: This is the scale-before-evidence error. Organisation-wide rollout of an untested change multiplies the cost of being wrong, and comparability is achievable within one team's own trend line.

options.text: Ask the team's most senior engineer to assess whether the proposal is technically sound before trying it.
options.rationale: This is the authority-as-evidence error. The two failed ideas were also technically plausible; what they lacked was measurement. Seniority predicts no better than enthusiasm whether a process change will move a metric.

options.text: Record the proposal in the improvement backlog and revisit it once current delivery pressure eases.
options.rationale: This is the defer-to-a-quiet-day error. Delivery pressure does not ease, and a filed proposal without a trial is how the improvement habit dies while the board stays tidy.

questions.explanation: Continuous improvement fails in two characteristic ways: adopting changes that were never tested, and never reviewing changes that were. The countermeasures are the two halves of the experimental method — define the measure and the success threshold before you start, and fix the date on which the evidence decides whether the change survives. Scaling prematurely, deferring to authority, and parking the idea each avoid one of those halves.

questions.stem: Your project is the fourth major change this year to land on the same operations department. The first three were each individually well managed, but usage data shows all three are being worked around, and your sponsor reports the department head as supportive in meetings while her team's adoption figures fall. Your rollout starts in six weeks. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: Adoption capacity is finite, and no single project can see how much of it is already spent.

options.text: Assess the total change load on the department with the other project managers and the department head, and take a sequenced recommendation to whoever owns the portfolio.
options.rationale: The pattern — three good projects all being worked around — is saturation, and it is invisible from inside any one project. Mapping the combined load and resequencing is a portfolio decision, so it goes to the level that can move the other three projects, not just this one.

options.text: Increase the engagement and training effort for your rollout so your project does not suffer the same fate.
options.rationale: This is the shout-louder error. It competes for attention in an audience that has run out of it, and the three predecessors were well managed too — effort was not the scarce resource.

options.text: Escalate the department head's contradictory behaviour to the sponsor as an adoption risk.
options.rationale: This is the misread-the-signal error. Public support with falling adoption is what an overloaded department looks like, not what a duplicitous manager looks like, and escalating her behaviour treats a capacity problem as a conduct problem.

options.text: Proceed as planned, since your six-week timeline is fixed and the other projects are outside your scope.
options.rationale: This is the not-my-portfolio error. The timeline being fixed does not change the department's capacity, and delivering a fourth change into a saturated environment produces the same workarounds the data is already showing.

questions.explanation: Change saturation is a portfolio-level phenomenon with project-level symptoms. Each initiative looks adoptable on its own business case because each was assessed as if it were the only demand on the same people's attention. The project manager cannot fix saturation alone, but can make it visible: quantify the combined load with peers and the affected manager, and put a sequencing choice in front of whoever can actually move dates across the portfolio.

questions.stem: A field service platform rolls out to 600 engineers in three waves. Wave one is live, and adoption splits three ways: a keen minority, a quiet majority waiting to see, and a vocal group posting workarounds. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: For the quiet majority, the most productive move at this point is to
For the vocal group posting workarounds, the most productive first move is to

options.text: make the keen minority's early wins visible in the engineers' own terms
options.rationale: The majority is not opposed; it is waiting for evidence from people like itself. Peer results in the language of the daily job move the middle far faster than another corporate message about benefits.

options.text: treat the workarounds as field intelligence and find out what failure they are compensating for
options.rationale: A workaround is a defect report in disguise: it marks where the platform fails the real work. Understanding it may produce a fix, a training gap closure, or a legitimate exception — and you cannot know which until you look.

options.text: announce a date after which the old method is withdrawn
options.rationale: Not used. A mandate can have its place late in adoption, once the evidence exists and the legitimate issues are resolved. Applied now it hardens the vocal group and tells the majority the evidence does not matter.

options.text: commission a satisfaction survey across all three waves
options.rationale: Not used. A survey measures sentiment at a distance, while the workable intelligence is specific: what the keen users achieved and what the workarounds are compensating for. Both are already observable without one.

questions.explanation: Adoption segments need different handling because they are different phenomena. The middle majority is swayed by peer evidence, not authority, so the enthusiastic early adopters are an asset to be made visible rather than merely thanked. The resistant minority is frequently the best diagnostic instrument you have, since workarounds cluster exactly where the solution fails the work. Mandating before the evidence exists spends authority you will need later.

questions.stem: Your product's recommendation engine, due for release in nine months, is built on a machine learning model. A draft AI regulation has been published that would classify engines like yours as high-risk, requiring documented risk assessments, human oversight provisions and dataset records. The final text is expected in six months, with enforcement twelve months after that. Your legal team is tracking it. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: A regulation that will exist inside your product's life is a design input, not a watch item.

options.text: Assess the draft's likely obligations against the current design with legal, and begin building the documentation and oversight provisions whose need is probable either way.
options.rationale: The timeline is the deciding fact: enforcement lands three months after release, inside the product's life. Work that is needed under any plausible final text — dataset records, oversight provisions — is cheap to start now and expensive to retrofit.

options.text: Monitor the regulation through the legal team and reassess the design once the final text is published.
options.rationale: This is the watch-and-wait error. It is passive in the face of a timeline that guarantees the obligation arrives shortly after your release, and it spends the six cheapest months the project will ever have for this work.

options.text: Redesign the engine now for full compliance with the draft text, treating it as a confirmed requirement.
options.rationale: This is the draft-as-law error. The text will change before adoption, and building to the current draft in full commits rework budget against requirements that do not yet exist — the opposite overreaction to monitoring.

options.text: Defer the engine's release until the regulation's requirements are settled, so the product launches compliant.
options.rationale: This is the pause-the-business error. It sacrifices nine months of value against an obligation whose final form is unknown, and a compliant-by-design build started now is almost always available without stopping the release.

questions.explanation: External regulatory developments sit on a spectrum between monitor and comply, and the position is set by two facts: how likely the obligation is, and when it lands relative to your product. Here the obligation is probable and lands inside the product's life, which moves it from a watching brief to a design input. The disciplined middle path is to build the capabilities that are needed under any realistic final text while legal tracks the variable detail.

questions.stem: Midway through your fit-out project, your organisation publishes a net-zero commitment that affects procurement: from next quarter, suppliers must report embodied carbon for materials above a threshold, and your fit-out will be among the first projects assessed against it. Two of your three material suppliers already publish the data; the third and cheapest does not. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: A new organisational commitment becomes a project requirement through the change process, with its consequences priced.

options.text: Assess the impact on supplier selection, cost and schedule, and bring the requirement into the project through change control with options, including engaging the third supplier on their reporting.
options.rationale: The commitment is external to the approved baseline, so it enters the project the way any new requirement does: assessed and authorised. Cost, schedule and supplier options all change, and the cheapest supplier may be able to comply given notice — all of which belongs in the evaluation.

options.text: Switch to the two compliant suppliers immediately, since the organisational commitment overrides the project's supplier selection.
options.rationale: This is the act-before-assessment error. It may be the right outcome, but taken unilaterally it reprices the project, possibly drops a supplier who could have complied, and makes a baseline change without the authority that owns it.

options.text: Continue with the current suppliers, since the commitment takes effect next quarter and the project's contracts predate it.
options.rationale: This is the grandfather-clause error. The project will be assessed against the commitment — the stem says so — so contractual timing does not shield it, and discovering that at assessment time forfeits every option except the most expensive.

options.text: Ask the sustainability team to handle the requirement outside the project, since it is their policy area.
options.rationale: This is the hand-it-over error. The policy is theirs; the procurement decisions, contracts and schedule it affects are the project's, and the two have to be settled together.

questions.explanation: Sustainability commitments made at organisational level cascade into live projects as new requirements, and they arrive through the same door as any other change: assessment, options, authorisation. The project manager adds value by pricing the consequences honestly — including the possibility that the cheapest supplier can comply with help or notice — rather than treating the commitment as either ignorable or automatically binding in its most expensive interpretation.

questions.stem: A newly formed team of eight has its first sprint starting Monday. Two members came from a team where estimates were commitments, two from one where the standup ran forty minutes, and one has never worked iteratively. The product owner wants to start sprint planning immediately to protect the first delivery date. What should the project manager do first?
questions.mindset: A team that has not agreed how it works will spend its first sprints finding out the hard way.

options.text: Hold a short working session for the team to agree its norms — estimation meaning, meeting discipline, definition of done — before sprint planning begins.
options.rationale: The three inherited habits described are precisely the disagreements that surface mid-sprint as friction if they are not settled first. An hour on norms is the cheapest alignment the project will ever buy, and it protects the delivery date rather than threatening it.

options.text: Start sprint planning as requested, and let working norms emerge naturally as the team delivers.
options.rationale: This is the norms-will-emerge error. They will — during sprint two or three, after the first avoidable conflict, and at the price of the early iterations the product owner is trying to protect.

options.text: Publish the working agreement yourself based on agile good practice, so no time is lost to discussion.
options.rationale: This is the handed-down-charter error. An agreement the team did not make is a document they did not agree to, and the members with strong inherited habits will simply run their own version anyway.

options.text: Ask the experienced agile members to brief the newcomer on how iterative delivery works.
options.rationale: This is the train-the-junior error. It addresses the least risky gap — the member with no habits to unlearn — and leaves the conflicting habits of the five experienced members untouched.

questions.explanation: Forming teams carry their previous teams' norms with them, and the conflicts that matter are usually between experienced members, not novices. A working agreement made by the team, before the first sprint, converts three private assumptions into one public set of rules. The time cost is trivial against the cost of discovering divergent expectations during the first commitment the team misses.

questions.stem: Two senior engineers disagree about the integration architecture for a component that enters build in three weeks. Each has argued their case twice in refinement, the rest of the team has stopped contributing to the discussion, and both engineers have now started lobbying you privately. The work cannot start until the decision is made, and both designs are credible. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: A technical disagreement that outlasts its evidence is a decision problem, not a technical one.

options.text: Convene both engineers with agreed decision criteria and a deadline, and have the team make or escalate the decision within that frame.
options.rationale: Two credible designs argued twice each means the disagreement is no longer producing new information. Criteria and a deadline convert the contest into a decision, and involving the team reopens a discussion the other six members have abandoned.

options.text: Choose the design you judge stronger, since the decision is blocking the schedule.
options.rationale: This is the referee-by-authority error. You are the person least qualified to judge between two credible architectures, and a decision imposed on its loser is relitigated at every future difficulty.

options.text: Give each engineer another session to present their case, so the team can hear the arguments in full.
options.rationale: This is the one-more-debate error. Each case has already been presented twice; a third round is an appeal, not a decision process, and the team has already signalled what further repetition is worth by going quiet.

options.text: Escalate the decision to the enterprise architecture function, since the team cannot reach agreement.
options.rationale: This is the premature-escalation error. Escalation is the correct end state if the framed decision fails, but jumping there now spends external authority on a disagreement the team has not yet been given a structure to resolve.

questions.explanation: Persistent technical disagreement between capable people usually means the decision has no agreed basis, not that one side is wrong. The project manager's contribution is structure: criteria the team accepts, a deadline the schedule needs, and a forum where the decision is actually taken. Deciding it personally, scheduling another debate, and escalating immediately each remove the structure or the team from a decision that needs both.

questions.stem: You discover that two team members have been drafting their status updates and some test documentation with an AI tool, then submitting them unedited. The summaries are fluent but twice this month they misstated which items were blocked, and one risk was described as closed while still open. The team has no agreement about AI use. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: The problem is not the tool; it is work leaving a person's hands that the person has not verified.

options.text: Raise it with the team and agree norms for AI use — where it helps, and the standing rule that the author verifies everything submitted under their name.
options.rationale: The failures are verification failures, not drafting failures. A team agreement keeps the productivity gain, names where the tool is useful, and fixes accountability for accuracy with the person whose name is on the work.

options.text: Ban AI-generated content in project artefacts until accuracy can be guaranteed.
options.rationale: This is the ban-the-tool error. It removes a genuine productivity aid, is unenforceable in practice, and addresses the instrument rather than the unverified submission, which is where the harm entered.

options.text: Speak privately to the two members and instruct them to stop using the tool for project records.
options.rationale: This is the two-people fix. Other team members are likely using the same tool or will next month, and a private instruction produces two compliant individuals inside a team that still has no norm.

options.text: Add a review step in which you check all status updates and test documentation before distribution.
options.rationale: This is the inspect-it-yourself error. It makes the project manager the verification layer for the whole team, scales badly, and transfers accountability for accuracy away from the authors, where it belongs.

questions.explanation: AI assistance shifts the failure point of routine work from drafting to verification, and teams need an explicit norm for it just as they do for any change in how work is done. The agreement should keep the tool where it helps and fix the one rule that prevents the observed harm: whatever carries your name, you have checked. Bans, private instructions and personal review all leave the team without that shared rule.

questions.stem: Your project is three months from delivery of a staff rostering system. The contract specifies the functionality in detail and the customer signed it. In conversation, the customer's operations director describes success as agency spend falling by a fifth within six months of go-live — an outcome that depends on how her managers use the system, appears nowhere in the specification, and has never been discussed with you. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: The specification is met and the project still fails when success was never defined the same way twice.

options.text: Raise the gap with the customer now, agree how success will actually be judged, and determine whose responsibilities — project's and customer's — the adoption side belongs to.
options.rationale: An outcome-based definition surfacing at month nine is an expectation risk with three months to run. Agreeing the real success measure and who owns the usage side converts an invisible failure condition into managed work — and it may require contract discussion, which is also better now.

options.text: Note the comment and deliver to the signed specification, since the contractual standard is what the project will be held to.
options.rationale: This is the contract-as-shield error. The specification may protect you formally, but the person judging the project has told you her actual standard, and a project that meets the paper while agency spend does not move will be remembered as a failure.

options.text: Add adoption support activities to the project scope so the agency spend target can be achieved.
options.rationale: This is the absorb-the-outcome error. It takes unilateral ownership of a result that depends on the customer's own managers, changes scope without agreement, and skips the conversation about whose job usage actually is.

options.text: Plan a benefits review six months after go-live at which the outcome can be assessed jointly.
options.rationale: This is the measure-the-wreck error. A review after delivery reports the gap; it does nothing to close it, and the adoption behaviours that determine the number are formed in the three months you currently have left.

questions.explanation: Late-surfacing outcome expectations are among the most dangerous project conditions, because the work being judged and the work being done quietly diverge. The project manager cannot make the customer's operations director adopt anything, but can refuse to let the divergence stay private: surface it, agree what success means, and settle who owns the human half of the outcome while there is still project time to act on it.

questions.stem: Your product owner has defined the first release of a booking product as fourteen features, and estimates seven months to deliver them all. Analysis shows three features account for most of the expected value and could be live in nine weeks. She is reluctant: a partial release, she says, will disappoint customers and burn the launch moment. What should the project manager advise?
questions.mindset: Value arrives when features do, not when the launch does — and it starts compounding earlier.

options.text: Propose releasing the three high-value features first, framing the decision as value timing: nine weeks of real usage and learning against a larger but later launch.
options.rationale: The comparison that matters is not small launch versus big launch but value in nine weeks versus value in seven months, plus what nine weeks of real usage teaches about the remaining eleven features. The launch moment argument deserves an honest test, not automatic victory.

options.text: Support the full-release plan, since the product owner owns release decisions and has given a coherent reason.
options.rationale: This is the deference error. The decision is hers, but the project manager's job is to make sure it is taken with the value-timing trade-off visible, and the current framing compares launch size rather than value arrival.

options.text: Escalate the release strategy to the sponsor, since seven months without any return is a significant business risk.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-before-advising error. The product owner has not yet been presented with the analysis that might change her mind, and going over her head first damages the relationship release decisions depend on.

options.text: Suggest splitting the difference: release nine features in four months as a compromise.
options.rationale: This is the split-the-difference error. It averages two positions arithmetically rather than examining the value distribution, and delivers most of the cost of the full release with most of the delay.

questions.explanation: Release scope is an economic decision disguised as a marketing one. Where value is concentrated in a few features, holding them back for a complete release forfeits months of return and months of learning from real users, both of which compound. The project manager's role is to put the timing trade-off in front of the decision owner in those terms — the decision remains hers, made on the full picture.

questions.stem: Your plan needs a data engineer at half capacity for the next four months. Her functional manager has offered her at full capacity for three weeks, then not at all, citing his own deadline. The project cannot absorb a three-week burst; the work is spread across the four months. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: In a matrix, you are buying a capability profile, and an offer that does not match it is a negotiation opening, not an answer.

options.text: Negotiate with the functional manager on the shape of the allocation — what his deadline needs, what the four months need, and what arrangement serves both.
options.rationale: The offer mismatches the need in shape, not in goodwill. Understanding what his deadline actually requires is what makes a workable pattern — adjusted timing, shared capacity, a second person for part of it — visible at all.

options.text: Accept the three-week full-capacity offer and compress the data work into that window.
options.rationale: This is the take-what-is-offered error. It accepts a resource shape the plan explicitly cannot use, and converts a resourcing negotiation into a schedule risk you chose.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the functional manager is withholding a required resource.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-the-first-no error. The manager has made an offer, not a refusal, and escalating a negotiation at its opening move spends senior authority and teaches him to route around you next time.

options.text: Recruit a contractor for the four months, since internal capacity is unavailable in the required pattern.
options.rationale: This is the buy-before-negotiate error. External hiring takes longer than the conversation, costs more, and may prove unnecessary once what the functional manager actually needs is understood.

questions.explanation: Matrix resourcing is a negotiation over the shape of capacity, and first offers are starting positions. A functional manager protecting his own deadline is acting rationally, and the productive move is to find the arrangement that serves both plans — which is only discoverable by asking what his constraint really is. Accepting the wrong shape, escalating immediately, and hiring externally all treat the opening offer as the end of the conversation.

questions.stem: At the current status date your project shows earned value of 240,000, planned value of 300,000 and actual cost of 300,000. Work out the schedule performance index and the cost variance, using a minus sign where a figure is negative.
questions.mindset: Indices tell you the rate; variances tell you the size. Report both or be misunderstood.

blanks.label: Schedule performance index, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 240,000 ÷ 300,000 = 0.80. The project is earning at four fifths of the planned rate — behind schedule.

blanks.label: Cost variance
blanks.rationale: CV = EV − AC = 240,000 − 300,000 = −60,000. The project has consumed 60,000 more than the value of the work it has produced — over cost as well as behind schedule.

questions.explanation: Reading EV, PV and AC together is the core earned value skill. SPI below 1 says the rate of earning lags the plan; a negative cost variance says the work done cost more than it was worth. The combination here — behind schedule and over cost simultaneously — is the signature that rules out the comfortable explanations: the project has not bought schedule with money or money with schedule, it is simply underperforming on both.

questions.stem: Your sponsor asks you to recover three weeks on a schedule with no float. Your analysis shows that overlapping the design and build phases — planned as sequential — could recover the time. The phases share the same four engineers, and the design phase is where most requirement defects are currently being found. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: Fast-tracking spends risk; the question is whether anyone has priced what it buys.

options.text: Present the overlap option with its specific risks and costs — rework exposure from unstable design inputs, contention for the same four engineers — and let the sponsor decide with the trade-off visible.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking is a legitimate technique and a risk purchase. The two facts in the stem — shared engineers and design-phase defect discovery — are exactly the price, and the decision to buy belongs to the sponsor, made with the price stated.

options.text: Implement the overlap, since recovering the sponsor's three weeks is the priority.
options.rationale: This is the obey-the-number error. The three weeks is the sponsor's wish, not an analysed decision, and implementing the overlap without surfacing its cost makes the risks yours rather than shared.

options.text: Decline the overlap, since overlapping sequential phases with shared resources is unsound practice.
options.rationale: This is the refuse-the-technique error. Fast-tracking is sometimes the right answer; dismissing it on principle removes a real option and leaves the sponsor's three-week need unaddressed by anyone.

options.text: Add two engineers to the team instead, so the phases can overlap without the resource contention.
options.rationale: This is the fix-one-risk error. Adding people addresses the contention and does nothing about building on design inputs that are still changing — and onboarding cost on a recovering schedule frequently erases the gain.

questions.explanation: Schedule compression techniques trade different currencies: crashing spends money, fast-tracking spends risk. Neither is right or wrong in itself, but the trade must be made explicitly by the person who owns the outcome. The project manager's contribution is the honest price list — here, rework from building on unstable design plus contention for the same people — after which the sponsor's decision is a real one.

questions.stem: Your organisation began publishing team cycle time six months ago to encourage faster delivery. Average ticket cycle time has improved 35 per cent, but release frequency is unchanged, defect reports are up, and ticket counts have nearly doubled. Which two conclusions are best supported?
questions.mindset: When a measure becomes a target, the number improves and the thing it measured stops being measured.

options.text: The improvement is largely an artefact of tickets being split smaller, which raises their count and shortens each one's measured time.
options.rationale: Doubled ticket count with unchanged release frequency is the fingerprint of splitting. Each smaller ticket cycles faster, so the average falls without any work reaching users sooner.

options.text: The metric should be paired with outcome measures — release frequency, defect trends — so the system resists optimisation of a single number.
options.rationale: A single published number creates a single pressure. Pairing flow with outcomes makes the gaming visible, which is precisely what happened here: the counter-metrics exposed the artefact.

options.text: The teams have genuinely become faster, and the rising defects are an unrelated quality problem.
options.rationale: This is the believe-the-target error. Real speed would show up in release frequency, and the defect rise is more plausibly connected than unrelated: smaller, faster tickets can mean thinner testing per ticket.

options.text: Cycle time should be replaced with lines of code per developer, which is harder to game.
options.rationale: This is the swap-the-metric error. It replaces a gameable output measure with an even more gameable input measure; the problem is single-number targets, not this particular number.

options.text: Ticket splitting should be prohibited so the metric returns to measuring real work.
options.rationale: This is the ban-the-symptom error. Splitting work small is often good practice; prohibiting it to protect a metric puts the measurement system above the delivery it exists to serve.

questions.explanation: Metrics published as targets reliably produce the behaviour that improves them, and the defence is structural rather than disciplinary: read every flow metric alongside the outcomes it is supposed to serve. Here the counter-evidence was already available — flat releases and rising defects — so the system diagnosed itself. The lesson generalises: never let one number carry an incentive alone.

questions.stem: Eight months into a fourteen-month project, the sponsor announces that corporate funding has been withdrawn and the project must close within four weeks. Two deliverables are complete and accepted; a third is two-thirds built. The supplier contract runs for another six months. What should the project manager prioritise in the closure?
questions.mindset: An early termination is still a closure: the same obligations, compressed, with less goodwill to spend.

options.text: Establish the disposition of the incomplete deliverable, settle the supplier position formally, and complete the acceptance records and lessons while the team still exists.
options.rationale: Termination adds two questions to normal closure — what happens to the half-built work, and how the supplier contract ends — while the standard ones (acceptance records, lessons) become harder, not easier, because everyone is leaving. All four need answers inside the four weeks.

options.text: Focus on the supplier settlement, since the deliverables already accepted speak for themselves and the incomplete one will simply stop.
options.rationale: This is the money-only error. The contract matters, but an undocumented half-built deliverable is a future liability nobody can later explain, and accepted work without recorded closure leaves its ownership ambiguous once the team disperses.

options.text: Use the four weeks to complete as much of the third deliverable as possible, so less work is wasted.
options.rationale: This is the sprint-to-the-wall error. A deliverable pushed from two-thirds to four-fifths complete is still undeliverable, and every day spent building is a day not spent closing — the work that determines whether anything built so far retains value.

options.text: Negotiate with the sponsor for a two-month extension to close properly, since four weeks is insufficient.
options.rationale: This is the fight-the-decision error. Funding withdrawal is not a negotiating position but a fact, and spending the first week of a four-week window arguing for eight weeks spends the scarcest resource on the least likely outcome.

questions.explanation: Early termination is closure under worse conditions: every standard obligation remains, two new ones appear (the incomplete work and the running contract), and the people needed to answer questions are already mentally elsewhere. The discipline is to treat the four weeks as a closure project of its own, with disposition decisions for the half-built asset, a formal supplier settlement, and the records completed before the team's knowledge walks out.

questions.stem: Your release depends on a partner organisation delivering an interface specification. It is due in four weeks; your build starts in six. The partner has delivered late on the last two occasions, each time by about three weeks, and their project manager assures you this one is on track. Your schedule has two weeks of float on this path. What should the project manager do?
questions.mindset: An external dependency with a track record is planned from the track record, not from the assurance.

options.text: Plan against the partner's demonstrated pattern — treat late delivery as the likely case, agree checkpoints before the due date, and prepare the fallback for the build start.
options.rationale: Two data points of three-week slips against two weeks of float means the probable case breaks the build start. Checkpoints convert the assurance into verifiable evidence, and a prepared fallback is what keeps a partner's slip from becoming your crisis.

options.text: Accept the assurance and monitor the due date, since the partner is best placed to judge their own progress.
options.rationale: This is the fresh-assurance error. The previous assurances presumably sounded identical, and a dependency with a demonstrated pattern is managed from the pattern — confidence that ignores history is optimism, not information.

options.text: Escalate the dependency risk to the sponsor now, given the partner's record of lateness.
options.rationale: This is the escalate-instead-of-manage error. The risk is real but currently manageable within the project — checkpoints and a fallback are available to you — and escalation is the step after those are in motion or refused.

options.text: Add three weeks of buffer to the schedule to absorb the partner's probable slip.
options.rationale: This is the pad-in-silence error. Three weeks of inserted buffer consumes float everywhere downstream, hides the dependency's real behaviour from the plan, and still leaves the build with nothing verified to start from.

questions.explanation: External dependencies fail predictably, and the prediction is the partner's history rather than their confidence. With a demonstrated three-week slip pattern against two weeks of float, the likely case already breaks the schedule, so the work is to verify progress at checkpoints before the due date and to have a fallback ready for the build. Accepting assurances, escalating prematurely and padding silently each leave the probable case unmanaged.
